title: Global burden of disease and injury and economic cost attributable to alcohol use and alcohol-use disorders

claims.statement: In the world's population in 2020, alcohol drinking compared with a counterfactual in which no one had ever drunk (lifetime abstention) is estimated by one modelling study to account for 741,300 new cancer cases (95% uncertainty interval 558,500–951,200), about 4 in every 100 new cancers (4.1%, 3.1%–5.3%; non-melanoma skin cancer excluded): about 6 in 100 new cancers in men (568,700 cases; 6.1%) and 2 in 100 in women (172,600; 2.0%) (Rumgay et al., 2021; no funding, no competing interests declared). The model counts only the cancers that the International Agency for Research on Cancer judges to be caused by alcohol: oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma only) 189,700 cases, 31.6% of all oesophageal cancers; liver (hepatocellular carcinoma only) 154,700, 17.3%; female breast 98,300, 4.4%; colon 91,500, 8.1%; lip and oral cavity 74,900, 20.2%; rectum 65,100, 9.0%; pharynx 39,400, 22.0%; and larynx 27,600, 15.0%. It attributes 346,400 cases (46.7%) to drinking more than 60 g of ethanol a day, 291,800 (39.4%) to 20–60 g and 103,100 (13.9%; interval 82,600–207,200) to less than 20 g a day (up to about two drinks), including 41,300 (35,400–145,800) to drinking up to 10 g a day, of which 24,600 were in women, 14.3% of women's alcohol-attributed cancers. These are model estimates, not counts of people whose cancer was traced to drinking: they combine drinking estimated from 2010 sales and surveys, assumed to act 10 years later, with relative-risk curves for current drinking from World Cancer Research Fund reviews of observational studies, applied in the same way to every country; former drinkers carry no extra risk in the main analysis; the uncertainty intervals carry only the uncertainty in drinking and in the relative risks, leave out that in cancer incidence, the 10-year delay and the model's structure, and are lopsided for the low-intake figures; and the hepatocellular share behind the liver figure comes from unpublished estimates. Adding stomach and pancreatic cancer raised the total to 808,700, and counting former drinking raised it to 925,900, though the increment the paper gives for this (135,000) does not match its own totals. Earlier global estimates cited by the paper, for other years and with other choices, were 5.5% of new cancers in 2012 and 4.8% to 4.9% of cancer deaths in 2016 and 2019; an earlier model by an overlapping team estimated 487 thousand cancer deaths caused by alcohol in 2004 (377 thousand in men, 111 thousand in women; no uncertainty intervals; Rehm et al., 2009); and in the Global Burden of Disease 2016 study, cancers made up 27.1% of the deaths attributed to alcohol in women aged 50 and older and 18.9% in men (Griswold et al., 2018). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.

In the world's population, alcohol use compared with no alcohol use is estimated by two global models to account for about 2.3 million (2004, after subtracting deaths the model counted as prevented; editors' rounding) to 2.8 million (2016) deaths a year. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016 (95% uncertainty interval 2.4–3.3 million), 2.2% of age-standardised deaths in women and 6.8% in men, about 2 and 7 in every 100; it ranked alcohol seventh among risk factors overall and first at ages 15 to 49, where 3.8% of women's and 12.2% of men's deaths were attributed to it, the leading causes being tuberculosis, road injuries and self-harm (Griswold et al., 2018; funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation). A WHO comparative risk assessment for 2004 estimated 2482 thousand deaths caused by alcohol, less 227 thousand deaths it modelled as prevented (215 thousand from heart and blood-vessel disease, 12 thousand from diabetes), leaving 2255 thousand, 3.8 in every 100 deaths worldwide (6.3 in 100 deaths of men and 1.1 in 100 of women) and 5.3 in 100 deaths before the age of 60; the deaths caused were mainly from unintentional injuries (666 thousand), heart and blood-vessel disease (545 thousand), cancer (487 thousand), liver cirrhosis (373 thousand) and intentional injuries (272 thousand) (Rehm et al., 2009; the underlying assessments supported by WHO and the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health; no conflicts declared). These are model estimates, not counted deaths: they combine estimated drinking (sales data, estimates of unrecorded alcohol, which is more than a quarter of the world's drinking, and surveys) with relative-risk curves from observational studies, mostly of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries, applied to every population. The 2004 estimate has no uncertainty intervals, and the 2016 paper does not say that its intervals include uncertainty from the model's structure or from bias in the underlying studies; the net figures depend on protective heart and diabetes estimates at low intake, which the 2004 authors call controversial; the 2016 figure is counted against a minimum-risk level of zero drinks a day, whose interval reached 0.8 drinks (10 g each) a day and which moved to about half a drink a day when the same group updated its weights (0.534, 0–1.00; Bryazka et al., 2022); the 2016 authors expect their figures to be underestimates, because drinking patterns, harm to others from violence and people under 15 were left out; and the two estimates used different methods and inputs, so the difference between them is not a trend. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
claims.magnitude: Griswold et al. 2018 (GBD 2016; 95% uncertainty intervals): 2.8 million (2.4–3.3) deaths in 2016; 2.2% (1.5–3.0) of age-standardised female and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; 1.6% (1.4–2.0) and 6.0% (5.4–6.7) of DALYs; ages 15–49: 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths; leading attributable causes at 15–49: tuberculosis 1.4% (1.0–1.7), road injuries 1.2% (0.7–1.9) and self-harm 1.1% (0.6–1.5) of total deaths; minimum-risk level 0 (0.0–0.8) standard drinks of 10 g a day. Rehm et al. 2009 (WHO comparative risk assessment, 2004; thousands; no intervals): caused 2482 (men 2039, women 443); prevented 227 (cardiovascular 215, diabetes 12); net 2255 (men 1944, women 311) of 58 738 deaths, 3.8% (men 6.3%, women 1.1%); under age 60, 5.3% (men 7.9%, women 1.9%); deaths caused by cause: unintentional injuries 666, cardiovascular 545, cancer 487, cirrhosis 373, intentional injuries 272, neuropsychiatric 135, perinatal 3. Bryazka et al. 2022: global minimum-risk level 0.534 (0–1.00) drinks a day with the GBD 2016 curves and GBD 2020 weights.
